units.text: Take the line y equals x, from zero to one. Square every height, and it sags. Higher powers sag further. Each curve is unbroken, from zero up to one. Pin one point, x equals nine tenths. Its heights go point nine, point eight one, point seven two nine, down toward zero. At x equals one, nothing moves. One to any power is one. So what shape are the curves heading for?

Flat at zero all the way to one, then a single point at height one. Unbroken curves, and a limit that jumps. A picture of a few curves can't prove that. Arithmetic can. Below one, each new power multiplies the height by the same number less than one.

Now let the point move. On each curve, mark where it crosses half height. There the curve is at one half and the limit is zero. As the power grows, the crossing creeps toward one, but the gap stays one half. So it matters who picks the point. Fix it first, and the gap shrinks to zero. Let it move with the curve, and the gap never does.

Shade every x where the curve is still above one half. That's a strip from the crossing up to one, and x equals one belongs to it. But at one, the curve and the limit are both at height one. The gap there is zero. So the gap is at least one half only on a strip that starts at the crossing and stops just short of one.
As the power grows, that strip gets narrower. Once it's thinner than a pixel, is the trouble gone?

No. Stretch the end of the interval sideways, ten times, a hundred times, a thousand times. The strip is still there. Reset the window to x to the tenth. Raise the power tenfold and stretch tenfold, then again. It looks almost the same. Its width shrinks like point six nine over n, and the strip is never empty. And the moving point is always inside it, with its gap of one half. A picture shows a few powers, at finite resolution. What we need is a guarantee for every point at once, and an order for who chooses what.
